readings.title: The expert's invisible pause
readings.instruction: Read the original passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A skilled assembler demonstrated a task without speaking. New staff copied her movements but often chose the wrong moment to tighten a part. She realised that she paused to feel resistance, a judgment invisible to observers. In the next demonstration she described that signal and asked learners to explain when they would proceed. Their actions became more consistent. Expertise included decisions that could not be learned merely by watching hands move.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节、推断与词义

readings.title: The mistake used twice
readings.instruction: Read the original passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A trainee cut a practice board too short. The instructor kept it as a teaching example, with the trainee's agreement, but removed his name. The class compared the marked line with the measurement record and found a unit conversion error. The board was then used to practise another joint. One mistake supported two lessons without becoming a public label attached to its maker. The instructor wanted errors to provide information rather than discourage questions.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节、推断与词义

readings.title: Evidence from everyday work
readings.instruction: Read the original passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Jon applied for credit towards a facilities course using his previous workplace experience. His first portfolio contained many photographs of finished repairs. The adviser asked for notes explaining the problem, his decision and the result. A tidy photograph could not show whether he understood why a method was appropriate. Jon added selected examples with supervisors' confirmations. The portfolio became shorter but more informative, linking claims of experience to the skills the course actually required.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节、推断与词义

readings.title: Practice before the busy season
readings.instruction: Read the original passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A repair team usually trained new workers during its busiest month, when mistakes were costly and explanations were rushed. The manager set aside two quieter mornings before demand increased. Staff practised common tasks on spare materials and discussed when to seek help. The sessions did not cover every possible situation. They established a shared starting point and a contact for unfamiliar problems. The manager treated training time as preparation for work, rather than time taken away from it.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：主旨、细节、推断与词义

translation.stem:
Translate this original passage into natural Chinese, preserving its meaning and logical connections.

Experienced workers often make judgments so quickly that they forget to explain them. A beginner may copy the visible movement while missing the reason behind it. Good instruction slows the process down enough to reveal those choices. When learners can explain why they act, they are better prepared to respond to a situation they have not seen before.
translation.referenceAnswer: 有经验的工人往往判断得很快，以至于忘记解释这些判断。初学者可能模仿看得见的动作，却忽略其背后的理由。良好的指导会适当放慢过程，让这些选择显现出来。当学习者能够解释行动的原因时，他们就能更好地应对未曾见过的情况。
translation.explanation: 参考译文不是唯一答案；信息完整、逻辑准确且中文自然的其他译法同样有效。

writing.stem:
Write about 120 words in English for this original simulation task.

Write a plan for welcoming a new colleague who must learn a practical workplace task. Include demonstration, supervised practice and feedback, and explain how the colleague should seek help.
writing.sampleAnswer: I would introduce the task in three stages. First, an experienced colleague should demonstrate it slowly and explain the decisions that are not obvious from watching. The newcomer should be encouraged to ask why a step is necessary. Next, supervised practice on spare materials would provide a chance to try the method without the pressure of a customer order. Feedback should identify one specific improvement and recognise what was done correctly. Before working independently, the newcomer should know which situations require stopping and whom to contact. A short follow-up meeting after the first week would reveal questions that did not arise during training. This approach gives the colleague both a method to follow and a clear way to handle uncertainty.
